name: Heap
tagline: Product analytics built on automatically captured events.
description: Heap is product analytics built on automatic event capture, so questions can be asked of data that was already collected.
pros: Auto-capture removes the instrumentation backlog: events are collected before anyone has decided which questions matter.
Retroactive segmentation answers questions from data that was already recorded, instead of waiting for a release to start collecting it.
Heap's value compounds quietly, because history keeps accumulating and later questions have more to work with than earlier ones did.
Funnels, retention, and cohorts all read from one captured stream, so the same event carries the same meaning in every view.
This dataset holds direct comparison records against Amplitude, Mixpanel, Matomo, FullStory, and Google Analytics, which makes a shortlist easy to build.
cons: Capture breadth creates a governance job: with every interaction stored, someone has to decide which events and definitions are trustworthy.
Retroactive questions only reach back to the moment Heap's script was first installed, and history from before that does not exist to analyze.
The recorded $5k-10k/yr band is an annual mid-market commitment, a different purchase from a site-traffic tool billed by the month.

content.title: Automatic event capture
content.body: Heap's central design choice is that interactions are collected before anyone decides which ones matter. Rather than a developer instrumenting each click, form submission, and page view against a written tracking plan, Heap's own script gathers activity continuously and leaves interpretation to a later date. That reverses the usual order of operations in product analytics: measurement first, questions second. The practical effect is that the size of an engineering backlog stops setting the ceiling on what a team is able to measure.

content.title: Retroactive analysis and the tracking-plan tradeoff
content.body: Because properties are stored as they are captured, an analyst can define an event today and apply it to history that already exists. A question that would normally start with an instrumentation ticket, such as splitting upgrades by the feature a user first touched, can be answered from what was recorded. The cost moves from engineering to governance: once everything is captured, someone has to decide which definitions are authoritative. Teams that skip that decision end up with several funnels that disagree with one another.

content.title: Analysis surfaces on the captured stream
content.body: Heap's analysis layer runs on a single captured event stream, so every item below draws from the same underlying record instead of from separately instrumented reports. This is what a product team usually asks for first, and the part that matters is that all of it can be pointed at events nobody planned when the script was originally installed.
items: Funnels built from any captured event, including ones defined after the fact
Retention and cohort views over that same event stream
Path analysis across the steps users actually took
Segments by user, account, or session context
Shared definitions so a reported funnel means one thing

content.title: The team that gets value from auto-capture
content.body: Heap fits product and growth teams that ask new questions frequently and do not want to queue behind an engineering release to ask them. The model rewards organizations willing to collect broadly and then curate, because auto-capture only shows its value once somebody is doing the sorting. A team with a fixed measurement plan of the same twelve metrics every month captures less of that value, since manual instrumentation would have covered those anyway. This repository's category listing places Heap across the SMB-to-enterprise range, which describes the dataset more than it guarantees a fit.

content.title: Pricing recorded for Heap
content.body: Our dataset files Heap as freemium with a list price band of $5k-10k/yr, and no exact current price is confirmed anywhere in our records. Separately, this repository's analytics pricing guide states that Heap offers a free tier covering 10,000 sessions per month alongside basic analytics features. The two records sit together without contradicting each other, but neither should be quoted to a vendor as fact. This assessment rests on Heap's own product documentation and the comparison records held in this repository; nobody here ran the software to produce it.

content.title: Connections to the wider data stack
content.body: In this dataset's comparison rows, Heap is marked present on the integration criteria against every product-analytics peer it is matched with, including Amplitude, Mixpanel, Matomo, FullStory, and Google Analytics. Those rows are generated checkmarks rather than measured tests, so read them as a statement that integrations exist rather than as confirmation that any particular connector was validated. What the record does establish is that Heap is positioned as one node in a stack: events arrive from the product, and analysis or downstream tools consume them afterwards.

content.title: Data handling and deployment posture
content.body: Heap runs as a cloud service, which means the captured event stream lives on Heap's own infrastructure rather than on the customer's machines. That shape has a plain consequence: retention, residency, and access decisions are questions for the vendor's documentation, not settings a team can settle locally. Nothing in the file assembled for this review records a compliance certification for Heap of any kind, and the machine-generated company record attached to this file is not treated as a source here. Readers running a formal security review should confirm current attestations with the vendor and read this gap as missing records rather than a missing attestation.

content.title: Peers in these comparison records
content.body: Thirteen comparison records in this repository pair Heap with other tools. Five of them sit in the same product-analytics field, namely Amplitude, Mixpanel, Matomo, FullStory, and Google Analytics, and those carry the signal for a shortlist because each is a different answer to the same question about measuring user behavior. Others pair Heap with website analytics or BI products such as Fathom and Tableau, where the useful comparison is scope rather than capability. The records that pair Heap with Mailchimp, Paddle, or Copy.ai mostly restate that tools in different categories serve different purposes, so weight them least.

content.title: Assessment
content.body: Heap is the right shape of tool for a team whose measurement questions outnumber its engineering capacity, and the wrong shape for a team that already knows exactly what it will track. The recorded rating of 4.2 from 1,380 entries sits below several product-analytics peers in this dataset, but those scores are directory figures rather than anything validated here. The decision underneath the rating is simpler: do you want answers drawn from data already collected, or a curated plan where every number was argued over first? Heap chooses the former.

faqs.question: What can Heap answer that a manually instrumented tool cannot?
faqs.answer: Questions nobody anticipated when the tracking plan was written. Because interactions are stored as they happen, a segment defined next month can be applied to data collected before the question existed.

faqs.question: What happens if Heap's script only covers part of the product?
faqs.answer: Only what is being captured can be analyzed later. Pages and actions outside the script's coverage leave no history to define events against, which makes install scope a data-quality decision.

faqs.question: What pricing does this dataset actually record for Heap?
faqs.answer: Freemium pricing with a $5k-10k/yr list band, plus a separate note in this repository's pricing guide of a free tier at 10,000 sessions per month. Neither is confirmed current; check the vendor.

faqs.question: Which products does this repository compare Heap against?
faqs.answer: Amplitude, Mixpanel, Matomo, FullStory, Google Analytics, Fathom, Plausible, Power BI, and Tableau, alongside several cross-category pairings that carry less signal for a product-analytics shortlist.

faqs.question: Does our dataset record security certifications for Heap?
faqs.answer: No. Nothing in our records captures an attestation of any kind for Heap. The product runs as a cloud service, so data handling and access controls should be confirmed against current vendor documentation.

author: Marcus Rivera
learningCurve: Moderate — reading reports is quick, while learning which captured events to trust takes longer.
whoShouldUse: Product and growth teams whose list of questions grows faster than their engineering capacity to instrument them, and who are willing to curate a broadly captured event stream.
whoShouldNotUse: Teams that need reporting on history from before Heap's script was installed, or organizations that only want page-level website traffic rather than product-level behavior.
